About

Distributed systems by trade. Machine learning since 2014 — classical, then deep, now agentic.

I build production LLM and agentic systems in Go, and the open-source tools that make them work. Most recently our production agentic platform on the Model Context Protocol — MCP server, execution loop, and tool layer, built from scratch — which turned days-long enterprise workflows into minutes of conversation and runs in customer environments today.

Under that: 10+ years as a Staff Engineer shipping distributed systems, security platforms, and Kubernetes infrastructure at scale — cross-platform fleet systems across 50K+ production endpoints, Kafka stream-processing pipelines, and ML data infrastructure on DoD-funded research.

Lately I'm channeling all of it into the open-source AI ecosystem — shipping tools developers actually use:

🔹 assay — Evaluation harness for MCP servers and AI agents · listed in awesome-go
🔹 research-agent-adk — Multi-agent research assistant over ArXiv and OpenAlex, with global rate limiting under parallel fan-out · Google ADK
🔹 testgen-loop-adk — Goal-driven loop agent that writes Go unit tests until coverage hits your target · Google ADK · Gemini
🔹 patents-mcp — Patent search via Google Patents BigQuery · listed in awesome-mcp-servers
🔹 immigration-mcp — US immigration guidance via live government data · listed in awesome-mcp-servers

    🤔 Prompt engineering taught us how to ask. Loop engineering teaches us how to delegate. Small autonomous systems with a goal — observe, propose, verify, iterate.

    Less theory, more code. So I built one. ⚡

    🤖 Meet testgen-loop-adk — a     Golang agent that writes unit tests until coverage hits the target. Built with Google ADK + Gemini.

    How it works:
     🔹 You set the goal. A small team of agents loops until it's met.
     🔹 Each iteration, three specialized agents work together — one observes the state, one (via an LLM, Gemini) proposes a change, one verifies and either accepts it or rolls back.
     🔹 The model proposes; the agents check its work. No manual prompting, no babysitting.

    Watched it climb: 0% → 33% → 50% → 67% → 83% → 100%. Five tests, ~13 seconds, zero prompts written. 💚

    👉 https://lnkd.in/dUtf8bVt

    Stars ⭐, PRs, feedback welcome. 🙏

    🤔 You shipped an Model Context Protocol server or an AI agent — but how do you know it still calls the right tools/sub-agents, with the right arguments, every time you change something?

    I'd built a few MCP servers (patents-mcp, immigration-mcp) and an AI agent research-agent-adk — and every tweak meant manually eyeballing that nothing broke. Python has DeepEval, Ragas. Golang had nothing standalone.

    🤖 Meet assay — an open-source eval harness for MCP servers and AI agents. Built in Golang, over a weekend ⚡

    What it does:
    🔹 MCP servers, zero code — assert the tools you expose and the results they return
    🔹 Agents, real checks — right tool? right args? right order? fast enough? expected output?
    🔹 Framework-agnostic core — knows nothing about any SDK, so a new framework is one thin adapter, never a rewrite
    🔹 Plugs into anything — adapters for Google ADK and the official Model Context Protocol Go SDK; bring your own in ~10 lines
    🔹 Deterministic & CI-native — MCP checks need no API key; every run exits with a real pass/fail code

    I dogfooded it against my own MCP servers and ADK agent — green across the board. 💚

    👉 https://lnkd.in/g8gkmSmB

    Stars ⭐ , PRs, and feedback welcome. 🙏

    🤔 What if AI agents could think 🧠, split work, run tasks in parallel, and remember your context — all orchestrated automatically?

    🤖 I just open-sourced a multi-agent AI research assistant — built over one weekend ⚡.

    During my PhD at     Indian Institute of Technology, Roorkee (2014–2018), I spent months searching, downloading, and summarizing hundreds of research papers. Each paper was a multi-hour investment just to decide if it was worth reading in full. That pain never left me.

    🛠️ This weekend, I built the tool I wish I had back then.

    research-agent-adk — a production-grade multi-agent research assistant using Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK) in Golang, powered by Google Gemini. Give it an ArXiv ID or a topic — it does the rest.

    What it can do:
    🔹 Analyze any research paper by its ArXiv ID — summary, key contributions, methodology and impact
    🔹 Search for papers on any topic and get a structured research landscape overview
    🔹 Deep dive into a paper — finds related work and profiles the authors, all running in parallel
    🔹 Remembers context across your conversation — papers you've explored, topics of interest

    Data sources: arXiv · OpenAlex — both free, no signup needed. Only a free Google AI Studio key for Gemini.

    I ran a live demo using the built-in ADK Web UI — screenshots attached showing all query types, multi-agent orchestration in action, and memory across turns.

    👉 https://lnkd.in/dp8up4UG

    This is just the starting point — the architecture is designed to be extended with new paper sources, new agent patterns, and new capabilities without touching existing code.

    If you're building with Google ADK, working on agentic AI, or just want to explore how multi-agent systems work in Go — contributions, stars, and feedback are all welcome. 🙏

    🚀 I just open-sourced two MCP servers — and they're both free to use.

    If you haven't come across it yet, MCP (Model Context Protocol) is     Anthropic's open standard that lets AI assistants like Claude connect to real tools and live data sources — turning them from chatbots into agents that can actually do things.

    Over the past few weeks, I built and shipped two servers in this space, both written in Go using the official MCP SDK:

    🔹 immigration-mcp — gives AI agents live access to US immigration data from official sources (USCIS, State Department). Ask plain-English questions like "What are the current EB2 priority dates for India?" or "My priority date is March 2015 — can I file I-485 this month?" and get accurate, up-to-date answers. It fetches the latest Visa Bulletin monthly and USCIS news daily. Informational only — not legal advice. 👉 https://lnkd.in/gn_ftN5Z

    🔹 patents-mcp — a patent search and prior art discovery server powered by the Google Patents public dataset on BigQuery (1TB/month free). Most existing patent MCP servers are paid, single-source, or unmaintained — this one is free, open, and built to be extensible. 👉 https://lnkd.in/gF95vcf8

    Both are MIT-licensed, production-grade (structured logging, graceful shutdown, unit tested), and ready to plug into Claude Desktop or any MCP-compatible client.

    This is just the start — more MCP servers and AI tooling coming soon. I'd genuinely love contributions: new tools, better prompts, bug fixes, or just a ⭐ if you find them useful. Issues and PRs are open.

    If you're working in AI, agents, or developer tooling — let's connect. 👋

July 31, 2026, Santosh worked with Tushar on the same team

I worked alongside Tushar on the CTAM project at FIU's Applied Research Center, and he was the person who fundamentally changed what our introspection platform could do. When he took over the system-call extraction work, the pipeline was pulling only a few hundred system calls per scan — nowhere near enough for the machine learning models to detect anything meaningful. Tushar rebuilt it from the ground up, modernizing the underlying Xen and libvirt stack and re-architecting how we captured data, and got us to hundreds of thousands to millions of system calls per scan. That wasn't an incremental improvement; it unblocked the entire ML side of the project.

What stood out beyond the technical result was how he worked. He took ownership of a genuinely hard, low-level systems problem, dug into the parts of the stack most people avoid, and kept iterating until the solution was not just working but scalable across concurrent VMs. He was also a steady presence for the team — someone the rest of us went to when something broke, and someone who mentored the newer researchers without being asked.

Tushar combines deep systems expertise with the kind of quiet reliability that makes a project actually ship. Any team building serious infrastructure would be fortunate to have him.

Deep Learning-based Cyber Security Solutions for Smart-City: Application and Review

Springer · Dec 8, 2021

Show publication

This book chapter provides the readers hands-on experience about the deep learning algorithms and their use case for cyber security solutions in the smart city ecosystem. In this book chapter, the authors first describe the background about the smart city ecosystem, cyber security threats and deep learning algorithms. Subsequently, the authors describe the overview of popular architectures of deep learning algorithms with their applications for addressing various cyber security threats. In this study, the author talks about convolutional neural networks (CNNs), fully connected convolutional networks (FCNs), Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), Deep Belief Network (DBN), Boltzmann Machine, and Auto-encoders.

Securing Environmental IoT Data Using Masked Authentication Messaging Protocol in a DAG-Based Blockchain: IOTA Tangle

Future Internet, MDPI · Dec 6, 2021

Show publication

The demand for the digital monitoring of environmental ecosystems is high and growing rapidly as a means of protecting the public and managing the environment. However, before data, algorithms, and models can be mobilized at scale, there are considerable concerns associated with privacy and security that can negatively affect the adoption of technology within this domain. In this paper, we propose the advancement of electronic environmental monitoring through the capability provided by the blockchain. The blockchain’s use of a distributed ledger as its underlying infrastructure is an attractive approach to counter these privacy and security issues, although its performance and ability to manage sensor data must be assessed. We focus on a new distributed ledger technology for the IoT, called IOTA, that is based on a directed acyclic graph. IOTA overcomes the current limitations of the blockchain and offers a data communication protocol called masked authenticated messaging for secure data sharing among Internet of Things (IoT) devices. We show how the application layer employing the data communication protocol, MAM, can support the secure transmission, storage, and retrieval of encrypted environmental sensor data by using an immutable distributed ledger such as that shown in IOTA. Finally, we evaluate, compare, and analyze the performance of the MAM protocol against a non-protocol approach.
